name: Slugging Percentage
summary: Total bases per at-bat. A single counts as 1, a double 2, a triple 3 and a home run 4.
easy: Batting average counts a single and a home run the same: one hit. Slugging adds up how many bases each hit was worth. A hitter with one home run in 10 at-bats is batting .100 but slugging .400.
Despite the name, it isn't really a percentage. It's average bases per at-bat, so it can go above 1, and in theory as high as 4.000, a home run every time up.

scale.note: Distribution of the 135 qualified hitters in 2026. Qualified hitters are mostly regulars, so the median sits above league average.

vars: at-bats (walks, hit by pitch and sacrifices excluded)

deep: Walks and hit-by-pitches aren't in it at all. OBP tells you how often a hitter gets on, slugging how far he goes when he hits, so the two fill each other's gaps.

Treating a double as exactly two singles and a homer as four doesn't match run values. In terms of runs, a double is worth less than two singles and a home run less than four. It's still easy to compute and good enough for a rough read on power, so it shows up everywhere.
Subtract batting average from slugging and you're left with power alone, singles stripped out. That's ISO.
